explanations.answer: Its wickedness has come up before Him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. God says, “…because its wickedness has come up before Me.” (Jonah 1:2) The text gives that one reason and nothing more, so I'm not adding a second one.

explanations.answer: Its king has turned his back on Him
explanations.explanation: I see why that one sounds official, friend. It's got a king in it, and kings sound important. But God's reason in this verse is that Nineveh's “…wickedness has come up before Me.” (Jonah 1:2) No king gets mentioned in it.

explanations.answer: Its people have mocked all His prophets
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic reason, baker, and it would make a great movie trailer. But it's not in the verse. God says, “…because its wickedness has come up before Me.” (Jonah 1:2) The text doesn't say anything about prophets being mocked.

Jonah does get up, I'll give you that part. Then the story takes a hard left turn. The text says he “…got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.” (Jonah 1:3) Nineveh was the plan, and Jonah went the other way.

Right on, baker. Jonah gets up, but not to go where God said. The text says he “…got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.” (Jonah 1:3) He heads for Tarshish, which is not Nineveh.

Tarshish it is, baker. The verse says it three times: Jonah “…found a ship bound for Tarshish.” and later he goes “…aboard to sail for Tarshish…” (Jonah 1:3) The man had his destination memorized. Too bad it was the wrong direction.
Egypt is a famous place in the Bible, but it's not on this ticket. The verse says Jonah “…found a ship bound for Tarshish.” (Jonah 1:3) Egypt doesn't come up in this passage at all, friend.
Tyre is a real city, but this boat isn't going there. Jonah “…found a ship bound for Tarshish.” (Jonah 1:3) Tyre never comes up in this passage.
Wind, baker. The text says, “Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea…” (Jonah 1:4) Such a violent storm arose that the ship was in danger of breaking apart. The LORD is the one who hurled it.
Fire would be a whole different kind of story, friend. And my ovens are the only fire I want to deal with. The text says the LORD “…hurled a great wind upon the sea…” (Jonah 1:4)
I get it, storms feel dark. But the text doesn't say the LORD hurled darkness. It says He “…hurled a great wind upon the sea…” (Jonah 1:4) The wind is what stirs up the violent storm.

True, baker. The text says, “The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god.” (Jonah 1:5) Each sailor calls on his own god, not all on the same one. That's a lot of different prayers going up.

That one's true, friend. The text says, “The sailors were afraid, and each cried out to his own god.” (Jonah 1:5) It wasn't one or two of them. Each sailor cried out, and every one of them was scared.

Cargo, baker. The sailors “…threw the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load.” (Jonah 1:5) That's a ship so desperate that it tosses its own stuff overboard. I've packed a cookie box too heavy before, but never like that.
Hold on to those oars, friend, because the sailors need them. Later they “…rowed hard to get back to dry land…” (Jonah 1:13) What they throw into the sea here is “…the ship’s cargo…” (Jonah 1:5)
Sails sound like a good guess, baker. But the text never says anything about the sails going overboard. It says they threw “…the ship’s cargo into the sea to lighten the load.” (Jonah 1:5)

Sleep, baker. Jonah “…had gone down to the lowest part of the vessel, where he lay down and fell into a deep sleep.” (Jonah 1:5) The ship is in danger of breaking apart, the sailors are throwing the cargo into the sea, and he's down there snoozing. I've napped in some wild places myself, but that's next level.

The text doesn't tell us Jonah's feelings, so I won't guess too hard. I think a man in a storm like that could feel all kinds of things. But what the verse says is that he “…fell into a deep sleep.” (Jonah 1:5)

Silence is close to sleep, but it's not what the text says. Jonah “…lay down and fell into a deep sleep.” (Jonah 1:5) The text says he's asleep, not just quiet. Big difference, friend, especially in a storm.

True, baker. The captain approaches Jonah and says, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God.” (Jonah 1:6) Honestly, I'd be asking the same question. The sailors are crying out to their gods, and Jonah is asleep.

This one's true, friend. The captain approaches Jonah and says, “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God.” (Jonah 1:6) The sailors are all crying out to their own gods. The captain wants Jonah's God in on it too.
They cast lots, baker. The sailors say, “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” (Jonah 1:7) No vote, no meeting, no committee. Just the lots.
A vote sounds civilized, friend, but that's not what they do on this boat. The sailors say, “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible…” (Jonah 1:7) They use lots instead.

The captain does speak up earlier, but not about this. He's the one who spoke to Jonah in verse 6. Here it's the sailors who say, “Let us cast lots to find out who is responsible for this calamity that is upon us.” (Jonah 1:7)
Not the captain, baker. The text says, “So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.” (Jonah 1:7) The captain can relax. Jonah, the one who was sound asleep, is the one the lot lands on.
False is right, baker. The lot doesn't fall on the captain. “…they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.” (Jonah 1:7) I bet that sleeping man woke up fast.

explanations.answer: The God who made the sea and the dry land
explanations.explanation: That's what Jonah says, baker. “I am a Hebrew… I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” (Jonah 1:9) Now notice what he says the LORD made: the sea. And the ship is out on that very sea.

explanations.answer: The God who rules from the temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's a different description of the LORD, friend, and it isn't what Jonah tells the sailors. He says, “I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” (Jonah 1:9) No temple and no Jerusalem come up in his answer.

explanations.answer: The God who led Israel out of the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: The Exodus is a big moment in the Bible, baker, but Jonah doesn't bring it up here. He tells the sailors, “I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” (Jonah 1:9) That's the way he describes the LORD to them.

Afraid, baker. The text says, “Then the men were even more afraid…” and then they ask Jonah, “What have you done?” (Jonah 1:10) They were already scared of the storm. Now they know the man on their boat is running from the LORD, and it gets worse.
I see why you'd think so, baker. “What have you done?” sounds a bit steamed. But the text says, “Then the men were even more afraid…” (Jonah 1:10) Afraid is the feeling the text gives them.
They did ask a lot of questions, friend, so curious makes sense. But the text says they were “…even more afraid…” (Jonah 1:10) Jonah had told them he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD.

True, baker. The sailors ask, “What must we do to you to calm this sea for us?” (Jonah 1:11) Jonah answers, “Pick me up…” and then, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you.” (Jonah 1:12) The sailors didn't come up with the idea. Jonah handed it to them.
It's true, friend. Jonah answers, “Pick me up…” and then, “and cast me into the sea, so it may quiet down for you.” (Jonah 1:12) Those are his own words. I think that took some nerve.

explanations.answer: They row hard to get back to land
explanations.explanation: Rowing first, baker. The text says, “Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not…” (Jonah 1:13) Jonah told them what to do, and the first thing they did was row for land. I think that says something about them.

explanations.answer: They tie Jonah to the mast
explanations.explanation: Tying Jonah down isn't what the text says, friend. It says, “…the men rowed hard to get back to dry land…” (Jonah 1:13) No mast and no ropes are mentioned.

explanations.answer: They cast lots a second time
explanations.explanation: The lots already did their job, baker. They fell on Jonah in verse 7, and the sailors don't cast them again. What they do next is that they “…rowed hard to get back to dry land…” (Jonah 1:13)

explanations.answer: Not to charge them with innocent blood
explanations.explanation: That's their prayer, baker. They cry out, “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood!” (Jonah 1:14) They're asking the LORD not to hold this against them. And I notice they're praying to the LORD now, not to their own gods.

explanations.answer: To carry them safely on to Tarshish
explanations.explanation: Tarshish was Jonah's destination, friend, not their prayer. They cry out, “Please, O LORD, do not let us perish on account of this man’s life! Do not charge us with innocent blood!” (Jonah 1:14) Nothing in it asks about the trip.

explanations.answer: To forgive them for casting the lots
explanations.explanation: Good try, baker, but forgiveness for the lots isn't what they ask. Their prayer is, “Do not charge us with innocent blood!” (Jonah 1:14) That's about what they're about to do to Jonah, not about the lots.

The sea doesn't keep raging, baker. The text says, “Then they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm.” (Jonah 1:15) The sea that had been raging against them grew calm. All it took was one splash.

False is right, baker. The text says, “…they picked up Jonah and cast him into the sea, and the raging sea grew calm.” (Jonah 1:15) So the sea doesn't keep raging after that. It grew calm, and that's after all that rowing.
Fear, baker. The text says, “Then the men feared the LORD greatly…” (Jonah 1:16) These are the same sailors who were each crying out to their own god at the start. Now they're fearing the LORD.

Vows, baker. The text says they “…offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.” (Jonah 1:16) That's a promise they make to the LORD. It's a big step for men who had each cried out to his own god earlier (Jonah 1:5).

Praise sounds natural after a calm sea, friend. But the text doesn't use that word here. It says, “…the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.” (Jonah 1:16)

I like the thought of sailors singing, baker, but the text doesn't mention songs. It says they “…feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.” (Jonah 1:16) Fear and vows are the words it uses.

Thanks would make sense, friend, but that isn't the word in the verse. The text says, “Then the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him.” (Jonah 1:16) The word that fits the first blank is fear.
